# Text as Data: Tokens, Normalization, Zipf {#sec-text-as-data}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** Every number and every code output on this page
was produced by running the code shown, with `scikit-learn` 1.9,
`tiktoken` 0.13, `sentencepiece` 0.2.2 and `tokenizers` 0.22; the full
environment is in @sec-setup. The `LogisticRegression` experiments here use
the default `lbfgs` solver. It draws no random numbers, so the
`random_state=0` in the code does not affect the result. Different library
versions or computing environments can still produce small numerical
differences. The chapter's interactive tools let you explore the steps of
tokenization, the Zipf distribution and relations in the vector space.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- turn raw text into model-ready units and defend each preprocessing choice;
- explain how byte-pair encoding (BPE) works, and use a given set of starting units and merge rules to work out how a new word is split into tokens;
- describe the distribution of word frequencies with Zipf's law and the growth of the number of distinct words with Heaps' law, and discuss what these patterns mean for building a vocabulary and representing rare words;
- derive a TF-IDF vector by hand and get the same numbers as `scikit-learn`;
- explain with examples what a bag-of-words representation keeps and what it loses, and justify in an interview which tasks it suits;
- explain how differences between languages, such as the agglutinative structure of Turkish, can affect tokenization, vocabulary coverage and token counts.

## The problem, in one sentence

The models we use in this chapter work on numerical inputs. To give them text,
we have to turn strings of characters into a numerical representation. We will
build count-based representations out of two basic decisions: [deciding which
units to cut the text into]{.hl} (tokenization), and [computing the value of
each unit in the document vector]{.hl} (weighting).

We will study this approach through bag-of-words and TF-IDF. These methods are
also a useful starting point for evaluating more complex text models.

This chapter builds **sparse** text representations. Only a small part of a
vocabulary built from a large corpus usually occurs in any one document, so
most components of a document vector are zero. @sec-embeddings moves to
**dense** vectors, which describe each word with far fewer coordinates, most of
them non-zero. Simple models that use sparse representations can be a strong
baseline where labelled examples are few, where long documents are classified
by topic, or where literal word matching matters. Such a model helps us weigh
what a more complex method gains against what it costs.

In building these representations we decide which units to cut the text into,
which differences to keep and which units to count. Large language models
involve similar design decisions; but when you use a pretrained model you
inherit a large part of them from the tokenizer that ships with it. This
chapter examines the options and the libraries' assumptions, to show how each
decision affects the representation.

**What we will look at.** First how text is cut into tokens, and the advantages
and limits of different choices of unit. Turkish examples show how those
choices affect the number of tokens. Then the distribution of word
frequencies, with Zipf's law, and the growth of the number of distinct words as
a corpus grows, with Heaps' law. Then we turn four short sentences into
document vectors in six steps and compute the similarity between them, showing
the intermediate results. Finally we discuss what information this
representation loses and why the next chapter moves to other representations.
On a first reading you can skip the collapsible "Deep dive" boxes and come back
to them later.

::: {.column-margin}
Preprocessing decides what information reaches the model, so it is part of the
modelling process. Treat the choices in this chapter as modelling decisions and
record your reasons for them. If you present your work in a paper, name the
preprocessing steps that affect the results in the methods section.
:::

## From characters to tokens {#sec-text-as-data-tokens}

::: {#gloss-tokenization .column-margin .term-gloss}
**tokenization** — cutting text into the tokens a model will process as
separate units. The tool that does it is a *tokenizer*. Where the units begin
and end is set by the method and the rules used. The structure of the language
affects how well suited and how efficient those choices are.
[↩](#term-tokenization){.term-back}
:::

::: {#gloss-token .column-margin .term-gloss}
**token** — an item the model processes as a separate unit. Depending on the
tokenizer it can stand for a word, part of a word, a punctuation mark, a space
or a sequence of bytes; it is not always a piece of text that can be read on
its own. There are also special tokens, used for functions such as marking the
start or the end of a sequence. In a service billed per token, the units
counted are set by the tokenizer of the model in use.
[↩](#term-token){.term-back}
:::

Before we can represent text we have to decide which units to use; this step
is called [tokenization](#gloss-tokenization){#term-tokenization .term-ref}.
The choice affects the size of the vocabulary, how new words are represented,
and how many [tokens](#gloss-token){#term-token .term-ref} a text is cut into.
In services billed per token, the number of tokens also affects the cost. When
you build your own pipeline, the sequence of steps that turns raw text into a
model's input, these choices are yours to make. When you use a pretrained model
you usually inherit the model's tokenizer. Either way you need to know what the
library does.

A simple place to start is to split the text at whitespace characters such as
spaces, tabs and line ends. In Python, `str.split()` with no arguments does
this. But it does nothing separate about punctuation, upper and lower case, or
suffixes. The example below shows which further decisions a task may call for.

```python
text = "The pump P-101 didn't fail; it's the seal (again!)."
print(text.split())
```

```text
['The', 'pump', 'P-101', "didn't", 'fail;', "it's", 'the', 'seal', '(again!).']
```

The output keeps `fail;`, `The` and `it's` as units of their own. `The` and
`the` both occur in it, and count as two different tokens. If another text
processed the same way contained `fail` or `it is`, those would be counted as
different tokens from `fail;` and `it's`. Whether such forms are counted
separately or mapped to a common form depends on the task. In deciding, weigh
which distinctions carry meaning and which only create an unnecessary number of
different entries for the same information.

This example shows the limits of splitting on whitespace alone. A tokenizer
that works at the word level can use separate rules for punctuation,
apostrophes, URLs, numbers and abbreviations. Normalization decisions, though,
such as mapping `The` and `the` to the same form, are separate operations from
deciding where tokens begin and end.

Even with a fixed word-level vocabulary, new text can contain words that are
not in it. We first look at how normalization brings different forms of a word
together, and then at how subwords are used to represent new words
(@sec-text-as-data-bpe).

### The normalization ladder {#sec-text-as-data-normalization}

::: {#gloss-normalization .column-margin .term-gloss}
**normalization** — in this chapter, the general term for operations that
reduce orthographic or morphological differences judged not to matter for the
task. Erasing case (*Pump* → *pump*) and mapping inflected forms onto a shared
stem or dictionary form (*pumps* → *pump*) are examples. The output of a
stemmer need not be the linguistic root. *Unicode normalization* is a separate
operation: it brings character sequences that look the same into one standard
form. [↩](#term-normalization){.term-back}
:::

The example above calls for three different decisions. Should `The` and `the`
be mapped to the same form? Should the semicolon in `fail;` be kept as a token
of its own, or removed? Should `it's` be kept whole, or mapped to `it is`?
These decisions affect case, punctuation and grammatical information,
respectively. Normalization can shrink the vocabulary by merging the counts of
some forms. Whether it erases a useful distinction has to be judged for the
task.

These operations can delete useful information too. Which distinction an
operation removes can be read from its definition; what that does to the task
has to be evaluated. The table below compares common
[normalization](#gloss-normalization){#term-normalization .term-ref} and
preprocessing options, with what each may gain and what it may lose. The table
is not a required order of application; stemming and lemmatization are in most
cases alternatives to each other.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**This table is for a pipeline you build yourself.** If the text is going into
a pre-trained model, stay with the tokenizer and the preprocessing assumptions
that model was trained under; adding the operations below on your own moves your
input away from the form the model expects.
:::

| Operation | [Possible benefit]{.pro} | [Possible loss or cost]{.con} | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lowercasing | `Pump` = `pump`: two columns merge into one and their counts add up. | `US` and `us` become the same form; the capitalisation that helps tell proper nouns and acronyms apart is lost. Python's `str.lower()` does not apply the Turkish mappings `I`–`ı` and `İ`–`i`. | Decide by language and task. Where a conversion faithful to Turkish spelling is needed, use a method that supports the Turkish letter mappings; with a pretrained model, follow the model's own preprocessing rules. |
| Removing punctuation | By removing selected marks, can match forms such as `fail;` with `fail`. | Deleting marks indiscriminately can change identifiers such as `P-101`, decimals, URLs and chemical notation that contains punctuation. | Instead of deleting in bulk, decide by task which marks to keep, split off or remove. |
| Stop word removal | Leaves the listed words out of the count. The English list used in this chapter removes 43.9% of all tokens, on the corpus and tokenization rule given below. | If `not` is on the list, negation can be lost; the content of phrases like *to be or not to be* changes too. | Measure its effect, especially with sparse count-based methods. Check that the list does not delete words that matter for the task. |
| Stemming | Can merge different word forms into one shared output. The Porter stemmer, for example, turns `replaced` into `replac`, and the Snowball Turkish stemmer turns `kitaplarımızdan` ("from our books") into `kitap`. | Can wrongly merge different words, or leave forms of the same word apart. In Porter, both `university` and `universe` become `univers`. | Try it in lexical search and sparse models; decide by looking at the outputs and at task performance. |
| Lemmatization | Aims to map a word to the appropriate dictionary form: `replace` for `replaced` used as a verb. | Depending on the method it can need a dictionary, rules, part-of-speech or context information. It can err on ambiguous forms; its cost depends on the tool. | Before adding it as an extra step for a pretrained transformer, check what input the model expects. Evaluate its benefit in sparse models and linguistic tasks. |

: The normalization ladder {tbl-colwidths="[14,26,34,26]"}

::: {.column-margin}
**What is Unicode?** Computers store text by encoding it as numbers. Unicode is
the standard that gives the characters of many writing systems shared numbers,
called code points: `A` is 65, `ç` is 231, `İ` is 304, `😀` is 128512. A sign
that looks like one letter on screen is sometimes made of more than one code
point. How code points relate to bytes comes a little later
(@sec-text-as-data-bytes).
:::

Start with the first row of the table, lowercasing: it needs care with the
letter mappings of the language. Python's `str.lower()` applies Unicode's
default lowercase mapping; it takes no locale parameter for Turkish. Turkish
has two separate mappings: `I` → `ı` and `İ` → `i`. The examples below show
how the default conversion departs from them:

```python
"İSTANBUL".lower()              # 'i̇stanbul': starts with U+0069 + U+0307; 9 code points in all
"İSTANBUL".lower() == "istanbul"  # False
"IĞDIR".lower()                 # 'iğdir' — should be 'ığdır'
```

These conversions raise no error, but they can produce unexpected results
downstream. Different spellings of the same word may fail to match, or the
tokenizer may split the word in an unexpected way. The default
`CountVectorizer`, for example, produces the token `stanbul` from the input
`İSTANBUL`. @sec-bake-off shows the problem on a corpus, and @sec-turkish-nlp
covers a conversion that suits Turkish. Once the preprocessing is fixed, the
vocabulary and the models that depend on it may have to be rebuilt.

The table's *Recommendation* column is a starting point. Each operation rests
on the assumption that the distinction it removes is not needed for the task.
Lowercasing, for example, can help in some topic classification tasks, and
removes a cue that comes from capital letters in named entity recognition
(NER). Take the model's requirements and the properties of the data into
account; compare the suitable options on validation data, and keep the test set
apart for the final evaluation.

Stemming and lemmatization are both used to gather different forms of a word
under one form, but they do not do the same thing. Stemmers such as Porter's
[@porter1980algorithm] apply rules aimed at inflectional or derivational
suffixes, and do not guarantee that the result is a word found in a dictionary.
Lemmatization aims to map a word to its base form in a dictionary, the form
you would look it up under: the infinitive of a verb, the uninflected form of a
noun. Some methods use tables and rules alone; choosing the right result for
an ambiguous form can need context. In English, for example, `left` can be the
past tense of `leave` in one sentence and the word for a direction in another.

The choice between stemming and lemmatization depends on your pipeline. With a
pretrained transformer, use the model's tokenizer and the preprocessing it
expects; do not add stemming or lemmatization on your own. Subword
tokenization (@sec-text-as-data-bpe) helps to represent rare or new words with
smaller units. It does not map inflected forms to the same dictionary form,
though: for the Turkish `kullanıyorum` ("I am using") and `kullandık` ("we
used"), for instance, it does not by itself create one shared column in a count
representation.

Stemming can help in lexical search or sparse classification, where you want
inflected forms gathered into one matching unit. But check which forms your
tool actually merges: the Snowball Turkish stemmer used in this book
(`snowballstemmer` 3.1.1) produces `kullanıyor` for `kullanıyorum` and `kulla`
for `kullandık`, and does not merge the two.

@sec-turkish-nlp runs a BM25 experiment with queries built from the target
documents, most of whose terms are in a different inflected form from the one
the document uses. In that experiment Snowball stemming raises the share of
queries whose target document comes first (recall@1) from 28.0% to 95.3%. The
result shows what stemming can gain in that experimental design; the same gain
should not be expected on real user queries.

::: {#gloss-stop-word .column-margin .term-gloss}
**stop word** — a word so common that some pipelines throw it away
before counting anything. *The*, *of*, *is*. Whether that is a saving or
a mistake depends entirely on the task. [↩](#term-stop-word){.term-back}
:::

::: {#gloss-vocabulary .column-margin .term-gloss}
**vocabulary** — the finite set of token ids a tokenizer can emit. A word
does not have to be in it whole: the tokenizer can split it into smaller
pieces that are. [↩](#term-vocabulary){.term-back}
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Weigh the information lost when you remove [stop words](#gloss-stop-word){#term-stop-word .term-ref}.**
`scikit-learn`'s English stop word list has 318 entries. In this chapter's 20
Newsgroups measurement, 311 of them occur in the corpus under the tokenization
rule used. They are about **0.4% of the [vocabulary](#gloss-vocabulary){#term-vocabulary .term-ref}**
(78,649 distinct token types) but **43.9% of all tokens** in the corpus. So
nearly half of the tokens are left out of the count. That share does not mean
the text shrinks by the same share in bytes, or the sparse matrix in memory;
the memory saved also depends on how many documents the removed words occur in.
And if a word that matters for the task, such as `not`, is removed, the
information needed to tell meanings apart can be lost.
:::

### Subwords: the compromise that won {#sec-text-as-data-bpe}

::: {#gloss-byte-pair-encoding-bpe .column-margin .term-gloss}
**byte-pair encoding (BPE)** — a way of learning the token list from the
text itself: start from single characters (or bytes), and keep gluing together
whichever pair occurs most often. [↩](#term-byte-pair-encoding-bpe){.term-back}
:::

With word-level tokenization, a fixed vocabulary may not cover every word form
met in new text. Character-level tokenization usually represents the same text
with longer sequences, and the model has to learn word pieces and words from
those small units. [Byte-pair encoding]{.hl}
([BPE](#gloss-byte-pair-encoding-bpe){#term-byte-pair-encoding-bpe .term-ref}) offers an option between the two by *learning* its units from data
[@sennrich2016neural].

See the three options on one word. Suppose `unbreakable` never appeared in the
tokenizer's training text. In the comparison we assume that the word-level
tokenizer has a fixed vocabulary and writes `<UNK>` (unknown) for words it does
not know. The character-level tokenizer's alphabet contains every character of
the word.

| Unit | How `unbreakable` looks | Result |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Word | `<UNK>` | The whole word is not in the vocabulary, so its spelling is not kept; the unknown-word marker takes its place. |
| Character | `u` `n` `b` `r` `e` `a` `k` `a` `b` `l` `e` | The spelling of the word is kept, in eleven units. The model learns the patterns inside the word from the order of those units. |
| Subword | `un` `break` `able` | The word is represented with three units. These pieces occur in other words too: `undo`, `breaking`, `readable`. |

: One word at three unit sizes {tbl-colwidths="[16,34,50]"}

The split in the last row is not made up: OpenAI's `cl100k_base` tokenizer cuts
this word exactly there. Which leaves a question: who chose `un`, `break` and
`able`? Nobody did. They were found by counting.

In this example BPE training starts by splitting the words into characters. To
each word we append `</w>`, a symbol that marks the end of a word. We count
adjacent pairs of symbols, weighting each word by its frequency in the corpus,
and merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol. Then we update the counts
and repeat. The code below makes ten merges. Which of several equally frequent
pairs is chosen first depends on the implementation; this code takes the first
one it met.

```python
from collections import Counter

corpus = {"low": 5, "lower": 2, "newest": 6, "widest": 3}
words = {tuple(w) + ("</w>",): n for w, n in corpus.items()}

def pair_counts(words):
    pairs = Counter()
    for symbols, freq in words.items():
        for a, b in zip(symbols, symbols[1:]):
            pairs[(a, b)] += freq
    return pairs

def merge(words, pair):
    a, b = pair
    out = {}
    for symbols, freq in words.items():
        new, i = [], 0
        while i < len(symbols):
            if i < len(symbols) - 1 and symbols[i] == a and symbols[i + 1] == b:
                new.append(a + b)
                i += 2
            else:
                new.append(symbols[i])
                i += 1
        out[tuple(new)] = freq
    return out

merges = []
for step in range(1, 11):
    best, count = pair_counts(words).most_common(1)[0]
    merges.append(best)
    words = merge(words, best)
    print(f"merge {step:>2}: {best[0]!r} + {best[1]!r} -> "
          f"{best[0] + best[1]!r}  (seen {count} times)")
```

```text
merge  1: 'e' + 's' -> 'es'  (seen 9 times)
merge  2: 'es' + 't' -> 'est'  (seen 9 times)
merge  3: 'est' + '</w>' -> 'est</w>'  (seen 9 times)
merge  4: 'l' + 'o' -> 'lo'  (seen 7 times)
merge  5: 'lo' + 'w' -> 'low'  (seen 7 times)
merge  6: 'n' + 'e' -> 'ne'  (seen 6 times)
merge  7: 'ne' + 'w' -> 'new'  (seen 6 times)
merge  8: 'new' + 'est</w>' -> 'newest</w>'  (seen 6 times)
merge  9: 'low' + '</w>' -> 'low</w>'  (seen 5 times)
merge 10: 'w' + 'i' -> 'wi'  (seen 3 times)
```

The first two merges build `est`, which in these words coincides with the
English superlative suffix. The third merges it with the end-of-word marker:
`est</w>`. Later steps build `low` and `new` as well. [The algorithm does not
recognise these pieces as stems or suffixes; at each step it picks the most
frequent adjacent pair of symbols.]{.hl} In this small corpus it helps that
some pieces coincide with morphemes, but BPE does not guarantee that they will.

BPE can also split words that are not in the tokenizer's training corpus into
learned pieces. To tokenize a new word in this example, we apply the merge
rules in the order they were learned:

```python
def apply_merges(word, merges):
    symbols = tuple(word) + ("</w>",)
    for pair in merges:
        symbols = tuple(merge({symbols: 1}, pair).keys())[0]
    return symbols

for w in ["lowest", "newer", "slow", "widest"]:
    print(f"{w:<8} -> {' '.join(apply_merges(w, merges))}")
```

```text
lowest   -> low est</w>
newer    -> new e r </w>
slow     -> s low</w>
widest   -> wi d est</w>
```

`lowest` is not in the tokenizer's training corpus, and yet it is represented
with two units from the vocabulary: `low` and `est</w>`. This is the main
reason subwords became common: **in this BPE setup, as long as the characters
of the starting alphabet remain available, a word never seen before can still
be built from those characters and their learned merges.** Some pieces, like
the `s` in `slow`, can stay single characters. Using smaller pieces can raise
the number of tokens; how that affects a language model's performance has to
be evaluated separately.

Notice the condition: every *character* of the new word has to be in the
alphabet the merges were learned over. Ours came from four English words. What
happens when a letter outside it arrives, a `ç` for instance?
@sec-text-as-data-bytes takes that up after the figure.

In training (top), the frequencies of symbol pairs are counted and an ordered
list of merges is built. In this small corpus the first three merges build
`est</w>`, which includes the end-of-word marker. That unit coincides with the
superlative suffix of the example words, but the choice rests on the frequency
of pairs, not on grammatical analysis. In inference (bottom), the learned list
is applied to a new word. `lowest`, which is not in the training corpus, is
split into the vocabulary units `low` and `est</w>` [@sennrich2016neural].
:::
::::

::: {.anlp-widget}
```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">Byte-pair encoding — type a word and watch the merges apply</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof bpeWord = Inputs.text({
  label: "Word",
  value: "lowest",
  placeholder: "try: lowest, newer, slow, widest, snow",
  width: 260
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Verbatim output of the merge loop at the top of this section — if the toy
// corpus changes, regenerate both together.
bpeMerges = [
  ["e", "s"], ["es", "t"], ["est", "</w>"], ["l", "o"], ["lo", "w"],
  ["n", "e"], ["ne", "w"], ["new", "est</w>"], ["low", "</w>"], ["w", "i"]
]
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bpeTrace = {
  const raw = bpeWord || "";
  const alphabet = new Set("deilnorstw");
  const invalid = [...new Set([...raw].filter(c => !alphabet.has(c)))];

  const trace = [];
  trace.invalid = invalid;
  if (!raw.length || invalid.length) return trace;

  let symbols = [...raw, "</w>"];
  trace.push({ step: 0, rule: "start (characters)", symbols: [...symbols] });
  bpeMerges.forEach(([a, b], k) => {
    const out = [];
    let i = 0, used = false;
    while (i < symbols.length) {
      if (i < symbols.length - 1 && symbols[i] === a && symbols[i + 1] === b) {
        out.push(a + b); i += 2; used = true;
      } else { out.push(symbols[i]); i += 1; }
    }
    symbols = out;
    if (used) trace.push({ step: k + 1, rule: `${a} + ${b}`, symbols: [...symbols] });
  });
  return trace;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div style="font-size:0.9rem;">
  ${bpeTrace.invalid.length
    ? html`<p style="color:var(--fig-warm);">
        This input contains characters that are not in the training alphabet:
        <code>${bpeTrace.invalid.map(c => JSON.stringify(c)).join(", ")}</code>.
        The input was left as it is and no merges were applied. This example
        supports only the lowercase letters that occur in its four-word corpus:
        <code>d, e, i, l, n, o, r, s, t, w</code>.</p>`
    : bpeTrace.length === 0
      ? html`<p style="color:var(--fig-muted);">Type a word made of letters from the training alphabet.</p>`
      : html`<div>
        ${bpeTrace.map(t => html`<div style="display:flex; gap:0.8rem;
             align-items:baseline; padding:0.22rem 0; border-bottom:1px solid var(--fig-border);">
          <span style="min-width:8.5rem; color:var(--fig-muted); font-size:0.82rem;">
            ${t.step === 0 ? t.rule : `merge ${t.step}: ${t.rule}`}
          </span>
          <span>${t.symbols.map(s => html`<code style="background:var(--fig-chip);
            border:1px solid var(--fig-border); border-radius:0.35em; padding:0.05em 0.35em;
            margin-right:0.2em;">${s}</code>`)}</span>
        </div>`)}
        <p style="margin-top:0.7rem; color:var(--fig-muted);">
          Final: <b>${bpeTrace[bpeTrace.length - 1].symbols.length}</b> token(s).
          10 merges were learned from this small corpus. Large BPE
          vocabularies hold far more; GPT-2's tokenizer has 50,000 merges.
        </p>
      </div>`}
</div>`
```

### Characters or bytes: what BPE starts from {#sec-text-as-data-bytes}

The example above started from characters. Tokenizers that use byte-level BPE,
such as GPT-2's and `cl100k_base`, start from bytes. To see the difference, we
explain the terms character, code point, character encoding and byte through
ASCII, Unicode and UTF-8.

A **character** is an abstract unit that text is made of; letters, digits,
punctuation marks and spaces are examples. `ç`, `a`, `y`, `7`, `?` and `😀`
are visible ones. But a unit perceived as a single sign on screen can be
represented in Unicode by one code point or by several.

Computers store text as sequences of bits. A character encoding determines how
the units of text are represented by those sequences. **ASCII** is a 7-bit
character encoding whose first version was published in 1963. Its 128 code
values cover the English letters, the digits, punctuation, the space and
control characters. The code value of the letter `a` is 97. ASCII has no `ç`,
`ş` or `ğ`, no Arabic or Chinese script, and no emoji.

**Unicode** is the standard that aims to represent the characters of different
writing systems in one shared system. The numerical positions in Unicode's code
space are called **code points**; encoded characters are assigned to them. A
code point is usually written as `U+` followed by the number in hexadecimal:
the code point of `ç` is 231, that is U+00E7. The 128 ASCII characters keep
their numbers in Unicode, so `a` is still 97.

A **byte** is the basic unit a computer stores data in. It is eight bits and
holds a number from 0 to 255, so it can take only 256 different values.
Unicode's numbers go far beyond 255, so a code point does not always fit in
one byte. An *encoding* decides which bytes store a code point. **UTF-8**,
which is widely used on the web, represents every encodable Unicode code point
with one to four bytes. Code points in the ASCII range are encoded as a single
byte, and larger values as two, three or four bytes, using bit patterns that
UTF-8 defines.

Here are all three side by side on the Turkish word `çay` (tea):

| | `ç` | `a` | `y` |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Unicode code point | 231 (U+00E7) | 97 (U+0061) | 121 (U+0079) |
| In the ASCII table? | no | yes | yes |
| UTF-8 bytes | 195, 167 | 97 | 121 |

: `çay`: three code points, and four bytes in UTF-8, when `ç` is written as U+00E7 {tbl-colwidths="[34,24,21,21]"}

In this spelling `çay` is three letters and three code points, and takes four
bytes when encoded in UTF-8. In Python `len("çay")` is 3 and
`len("çay".encode("utf-8"))` is 4. Text that looks the same can also be written
with a different sequence of code points: write `c` followed by a separate
cedilla mark instead of `ç`, and the same word is four code points and five
bytes. These numbers depend on the Unicode spelling and on the encoding.

Why does a tokenizer care? Because the symbols BPE starts merging from are
either characters or bytes, and there are very different *numbers* of each:

- **A character alphabet can be large.** Unicode's code space is finite, but it
  holds a great many characters, and new versions define new ones. A
  tokenizer's starting alphabet can be chosen from the training data;
  characters can be added to it, or its coverage limited. A character that is
  not in that alphabet needs an extra mechanism, such as an unknown token or a
  fallback to bytes.
- **A byte alphabet can be complete with 256 values.** If the starting alphabet
  contains every byte value, every byte of UTF-8 encoded text can be
  represented. The bytes of a new character then need no new starting symbol.

The rest of this section works through the two options and what each costs.

First a short note on history. The loop above — count adjacent pairs, merge the
most frequent, repeat — *is* BPE. The name is older than its use in NLP: it comes from a 1994 data-compression
algorithm that kept replacing the most frequent pair of adjacent **bytes** in a
file with a single byte value the file did not use [@gage1994new]. Sennrich and
colleagues kept the loop and changed its purpose: the merges build a vocabulary
instead of shrinking a file, and the merge list is kept so it can be replayed
on new text [@sennrich2016neural].

That leaves one decision the loop does not make for you: **what the starting
symbols are**. Do not confuse it with the choice of algorithm; the two are
separate decisions. BPE is not the only way to learn a subword vocabulary. You
will meet two relatives of it later: **WordPiece**, which BERT uses, and
**Unigram**, which T5 uses. All three are used to build subword vocabularies,
but they differ in how the vocabulary is learned and in how new text is split
into pieces. Our main example here is BPE. WordPiece and Unigram come up in a
"Deep dive" box in this chapter (@sec-text-as-data-granularities), and the
methods are compared in more detail where we look at BERT's tokenizer
(@sec-tokenizer-algorithms). What you need for now:
the algorithm decides *how* units are learned. Characters or bytes decide *what
they are built from*, and that question is the same for all three algorithms.

**Starting from characters.** This is what the example above did. The merge
table can only combine symbols it has seen, and the alphabet this one saw came
from four English words. `apply_merges("çay", merges)` returns
`('ç', 'a', 'y', '</w>')`. But `ç`, `a` and `y` are not in the starting
alphabet built from this small corpus. The function only applies merge rules
and does not check for symbols outside the vocabulary, so it leaves them in the
output. A usable tokenizer has to handle this case separately: it can add the
characters to its starting alphabet, use an unknown token (`<UNK>`), or fall
back to bytes. That a character is rare does not mean it must become an
unknown token.

**Starting from bytes.** The other option is to start from the UTF-8 bytes of
the characters instead of the characters themselves. UTF-8 represents every
encodable Unicode code point with one to four bytes. ASCII letters take one
byte. In the spellings below, each of the Turkish letters `ç`, `ş`, `ğ`, `ı`,
`ö`, `ü` and `İ` is two bytes; `世` is three and `😀` is four. Emoji and other
combined spellings made of more than one code point can be longer than four
bytes in total:

```python
for ch in ["a", "ç", "ş", "İ", "世", "😀"]:
    b = ch.encode("utf-8")
    print(f"{ch}  U+{ord(ch):04X}  {len(b)} byte(s): {' '.join(f'{x:02X}' for x in b)}")
```

```text
a  U+0061  1 byte(s): 61
ç  U+00E7  2 byte(s): C3 A7
ş  U+015F  2 byte(s): C5 9F
İ  U+0130  2 byte(s): C4 B0
世  U+4E16  3 byte(s): E4 B8 96
😀  U+1F600  4 byte(s): F0 9F 98 80
```

A byte has only 256 possible values, so an alphabet of 256 bytes is closed:
every string in every language is a sequence of them. Byte-level BPE runs
exactly the same merge loop over byte sequences instead of characters
[@radford2019language]. At each step the loop merges the most frequent
adjacent pair of symbols. Some characters and word pieces can end up
represented as single tokens that way. The two bytes of `ç`, for example, can
become one token; whether that happens, and at which step, depends on the
frequencies in the training data and on the number of merges made.
But [the merges are not bound to Unicode character boundaries]{.hl}: the
algorithm does not know where a character ends, only which byte pair is
frequent. So a token can stand for a whole character, for several characters,
or for only part of one UTF-8 character. The next output shows all three.

Here is a byte-level tokenizer, OpenAI's `cl100k_base`, showing the bytes behind
each token. `enc.encode` returns the token ids as a list of integers. Text is
passed to the model through those ids. `decode_single_token_bytes` shows the
sequence of bytes each id stands for:

```python
import tiktoken

enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")
for text in ["çay", "şişe", "ŞİŞE", "😀"]:
    pieces = [enc.decode_single_token_bytes(t) for t in enc.encode(text)]
    print(f"{text:<5} {len(pieces)} tokens  {pieces}")
```

```text
çay   2 tokens  [b'\xc3\xa7', b'ay']
şişe  3 tokens  [b'\xc5\x9fi', b'\xc5\x9f', b'e']
ŞİŞE  6 tokens  [b'\xc5', b'\x9e', b'\xc4\xb0', b'\xc5', b'\x9e', b'E']
😀     2 tokens  [b'\xf0\x9f\x98', b'\x80']
```

In this output the two bytes of `ç` sit in a single token. `ŞİŞE` produces six
tokens and `şişe` three. The two bytes of capital `Ş` are split over separate
tokens, while `İ` and `E` stay whole. From this output alone we cannot tell how
often `Ş` occurred in the training data. `b'\xc5'` is not a valid UTF-8
sequence on its own; it has to be joined with the next byte before the
character can be read. `😀` is split into two tokens as well: the first holds
three bytes and the second the last one. None of these examples needs an
unknown token; but the same number of visible characters can produce different
numbers of tokens.

In the table below, "character" means a Unicode code point. The byte-level
column assumes that the starting alphabet contains all 256 byte values.

| | BPE starting from characters | BPE starting from bytes |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Starting alphabet | Selected code points; they can be taken from the training data or added separately. | The 256 byte values. |
| A character that is not in the starting alphabet | [Needs an extra mechanism, such as an unknown token or the byte fallback below.]{.con} | [Represented by its UTF-8 bytes.]{.pro} |
| What does one token stand for? | [One or more whole code points.]{.pro} | [A sequence of bytes; sometimes only part of the UTF-8 form of a code point.]{.con} |
| Cost of a code point that is not merged into a larger piece | [One token, if it is in the alphabet.]{.pro} | [One to four tokens, depending on its UTF-8 form and on the learned merges.]{.con} |
| Coverage | Limited to the chosen alphabet and to the fallback mechanism, if there is one. | Covers every byte of UTF-8 encoded text. |

: Characters or bytes as the starting alphabet {tbl-colwidths="[26,37,37]"}

A third design combines the two: **byte fallback**, which means spelling an
unknown character out in bytes. The vocabulary is still built from characters
and their merges, but one token for each of the 256 byte values is added to it.
The tokenizer handles the characters it knows as usual. When it meets one it
does not know, it writes that character's UTF-8 bytes one by one with those
byte tokens instead of writing `<UNK>`. The SentencePiece library offers this
as an option (`byte_fallback=True`).

A small experiment shows it. Below, SentencePiece is trained twice on eight
Turkish words that contain no `ç`: once with the option off and once with it
on. Both models are then given the word `çay`:

```python
import sentencepiece as spm

words = ["ev", "evde", "evden", "evler", "yol", "yolda", "yoldan", "yollar"]
with open("mini.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("\n".join(words * 5) + "\n")            # no 'ç' anywhere in this text

for fallback in [False, True]:
    spm.SentencePieceTrainer.train(
        input="mini.txt", model_prefix="mini", model_type="bpe",
        vocab_size=20 + (256 if fallback else 0), byte_fallback=fallback,
        character_coverage=1.0, hard_vocab_limit=False, minloglevel=2,
        bos_id=-1, eos_id=-1, pad_id=-1)
    sp = spm.SentencePieceProcessor(model_file="mini.model")
    ids = sp.encode("çay")
    print(f"byte_fallback={fallback!s:<5}  vocabulary {sp.get_piece_size():>3}  "
          f"{sp.encode('çay', out_type=str)}  ->  {sp.decode(ids)!r}")
```

```text
byte_fallback=False  vocabulary  20  ['▁', 'ç', 'a', 'y']  ->  ' ⁇ ay'
byte_fallback=True   vocabulary 276  ['▁', '<0xC3>', '<0xA7>', 'a', 'y']  ->  'çay'
```

In the first line `ç` is not in the vocabulary and is encoded with the unknown
token's id. The list of pieces still shows `ç`, because that list prints the
unknown piece as it is spelled in the text. It does not mean the vocabulary has
an entry for `ç`. When the ids are turned back into text, a `⁇` mark takes the
letter's place.

In the second line the vocabulary has grown from 20 to 276 with the 256 added
byte tokens. `ç` is represented as `<0xC3>` and `<0xA7>`. Those are the two
bytes from the table above: hexadecimal C3 is 195 and A7 is 167. Turned back
into text from the ids, `çay` comes out intact. The leading `▁` is the mark
SentencePiece uses to make a space visible. Here it stands for the space that
the default setting adds in front of the text; the next section comes back to
this notation.

**Which one is used today.** Many GPT-type models use byte-level BPE or a
variant of it. Other model families also use WordPiece and Unigram.
SentencePiece is a library that can train a tokenizer with either BPE or
Unigram. GPT-2 introduced byte-level BPE with a
50,257-token vocabulary [@radford2019language]. OpenAI's `cl100k_base` and
`o200k_base`, measured in the next section, are byte-level. Llama 3 moved to a
128K-token vocabulary that combines 100K tokens from OpenAI's `tiktoken` with 28K
added for non-English languages [@grattafiori2024llama3]. BERT and its close
relatives such as DistilBERT and ELECTRA still ship WordPiece over characters
[@devlin2019bert] (RoBERTa, although built on BERT, switched to GPT-2's
byte-level BPE), and a later
table (@sec-tokenizer-algorithms) shows which algorithm ships where. The
practical rule does not depend on any of this: use the tokenizer the model was
trained with, and count tokens with it.

Coverage and token count have to be kept apart here. If the starting alphabet
contains all 256 byte values, no unknown token is needed to represent the bytes
of a Turkish word encoded in UTF-8. That does not mean the normalization that
runs before tokenization preserves the original text: letters it changed or
spaces it deleted cannot be brought back by byte coverage.

How many tokens a text produces depends on the training data, the learned
merges, and the size and content of the vocabulary. No separate vocabulary
quota needs to have been set for each language. The next section measures this
difference in token counts on Turkish examples.

**This section in short.** The coverage of BPE that starts from characters
depends on the chosen starting alphabet and on extra mechanisms such as byte
fallback, if there are any. BPE that starts from all 256 byte values can
represent the bytes of any UTF-8 encoded text. In return, some code points can
be split over more than one token. In both approaches the number of tokens
depends on the learned vocabulary and on the content of the text.

### Who pays for Turkish {#sec-text-as-data-turkish}

A tokenizer can produce different numbers of tokens for the same content in
different languages. The difference depends on the language mix and the content
of the training corpus, on the vocabulary size, on the tokenization algorithm
and on the preprocessing rules. Let us look at the difference between Turkish
and English on a concrete example. Here is Article 1 of the Universal
Declaration of Human Rights, in the official English and Turkish texts, run
through OpenAI's tokenizers:

```python
import tiktoken

en = ("All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. "
      "They are endowed with reason and conscience and should act towards "
      "one another in a spirit of brotherhood.")
tr = ("Bütün insanlar hür, haysiyet ve haklar bakımından eşit doğarlar. "
      "Akıl ve vicdana sahiptirler ve birbirlerine karşı kardeşlik "
      "zihniyeti ile hareket etmelidirler.")

for name in ["cl100k_base", "o200k_base"]:
    enc = tiktoken.get_encoding(name)
    a, b = len(enc.encode(en)), len(enc.encode(tr))
    print(f"{name}:")
    print(f"  english : {len(en):>4} code points -> {a:>3} tokens  "
          f"({len(en) / a:4.2f} code points/token)")
    print(f"  turkish : {len(tr):>4} code points -> {b:>3} tokens  "
          f"({len(tr) / b:4.2f} code points/token)")
    print(f"  Turkish/English token count ratio: {b / a:4.2f}")
```

```text
cl100k_base:
  english :  170 code points ->  33 tokens  (5.15 code points/token)
  turkish :  160 code points ->  60 tokens  (2.67 code points/token)
  Turkish/English token count ratio: 1.82
o200k_base:
  english :  170 code points ->  33 tokens  (5.15 code points/token)
  turkish :  160 code points ->  46 tokens  (3.48 code points/token)
  Turkish/English token count ratio: 1.39
```

In these two-sentence texts of the same article, the Turkish token count is
[about 1.82 times]{.hl} the English one with `cl100k_base`, and 1.39 times with
`o200k_base`. In this example the second encoding narrows the difference.

In a comparison where the same input price per token applies, more tokens mean
a higher input cost. A fixed token limit can also correspond to different
amounts of content in texts like these. The total cost, though, depends on the
model chosen, on the lengths of input and output, and on the pricing terms.

Similar differences between languages have been shown in broader studies
[@petrov2023language]. The two texts here do not give a universal ratio for
Turkish. Nor is it enough to explain the difference by some Turkish letters
taking two bytes in UTF-8; the learned vocabulary and the tokenization rules
act together.

Where does the difference come from? Turkish encodes far more grammatical
information inside a single word, with suffixes, than English does
[@oflazer1994two], so one stem produces many surface forms. English expresses
the same grammatical information with separate words in some constructions. If
those words are frequent in the training corpus, they can be represented with
short token sequences. In Turkish, how the many inflected forms are split
depends on which shared sequences the tokenizer has learned.

Below you can see how the output of `cl100k_base` changes as suffixes are added
to the stem `ev` ("house"). We encoded each word separately, with a single
space in front of it:

```text
ev             1 tokens  [' ev']
evler          2 tokens  [' ev', 'ler']
evlerimiz      4 tokens  [' ev', 'ler', 'im', 'iz']
evlerimizden   5 tokens  [' ev', 'ler', 'im', 'iz', 'den']
```
